target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and reliably increase voting access.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably solve access problems because private employers are generally not required to close or give paid leave, so retail, hospitality, healthcare, and other service workers could still be scheduled to work and lose wages or be unable to vote during polling hours. The policy therefore does not reliably produce the day off from work that AG1 assumes, especially for low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would not consistently remove access barriers because not all employers must close or provide paid leave.
objection: Even without a legal requirement that every private employer close, a national holiday still meaningfully reduces scheduling barriers: it changes the default calendar, schools are closed, and many workplaces adjust holiday staffing and become more willing to accommodate voting. The objection overstates the need for universal paid leave in order for the holiday to improve access.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would not meaningfully help low-income hourly workers because it would not force paid leave or wage protection.
objection: The relevant barrier is not only whether employers must give paid time off. Holiday status can still reduce the wage-loss penalty because many employers pay holiday premiums or use different staffing norms, so hourly workers are less exposed to the same economic cost they face on an ordinary weekday.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status would reduce the wage and schedule burden for low-income workers even without mandatory paid leave.
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee holiday premiums, compensatory time, or paid leave in private-sector service and retail jobs, so low-income hourly workers can still be scheduled to work with the same wage-loss pressure. The holiday label alone does not reliably reduce their real cost of voting.

target: AG2's claim that holiday status does not reliably lower the burden on low-income workers because it does not mandate paid leave.
objection: The schedule barrier is broader than paid-leave policy: low-income workers often face a combined work-and-childcare problem. Making Election Day a holiday changes the school and caregiving calendar, which can remove the childcare/school conflict that otherwise prevents parents from voting, even if their employer does not provide paid leave.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would reliably change the school and childcare schedule in ways that help parents vote.
objection: Federal holiday status does not compel schools to close or childcare providers to stop operating, and many private childcare arrangements can remain open or still require payment. Because the holiday does not control these schedules, it cannot be assumed to consistently remove the school/childcare conflict that AG1 relies on.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday cannot reliably remove school/childcare conflicts because it does not force every provider to close.
objection: For many voters, the relevant issue is the school-day baseline, not universal closure of every childcare provider. Public schools commonly close on federal holidays, and many childcare arrangements depend on the school calendar, so the holiday still meaningfully eases the childcare and school schedule conflict that blocks voting.

target: AG2's claim that parents cannot rely on holiday status to solve childcare conflicts because every provider need not close.
objection: Even if childcare centers stay open, a national holiday can still lower childcare conflicts because more potential backup caregivers—relatives, grandparents, partners, and others—are more likely to be off work. That makes it easier for parents to arrange care during polling hours without needing the federal government to control every provider's schedule.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status makes backup caregivers more available and therefore reduces parents' childcare problems.
objection: Backup caregivers are not guaranteed to be available on a federal holiday, because many of them also work hourly jobs that may still be scheduled. Holiday designation does not ensure paid leave, does not provide money for substitute care, and does not remove the parent's own work-time constraint, so the claimed reduction in childcare problems is unreliable.

target: AG1's claim that an election holiday is a reliable turnout strategy and a worthwhile policy compared with other reforms.
objection: Research shows that having an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise voter turnout relative to other voting-access reforms. State laws requiring time off to vote or measures like automatic voter registration have a more direct causal link to participation, so a holiday is a weaker policy choice.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday alone is ineffective and does not reliably improve access.
objection: The holiday changes the school/work calendar that creates the main barrier, especially for students and parents, and it also shifts workplace norms and expectations on that day. That means the policy directly reduces scheduling friction and is not merely symbolic, even if it does not guarantee universal paid leave.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is too weak because it does not guarantee paid protected time for every worker.
objection: The policy's purpose is to remove rigid schedule conflicts, not to guarantee perfect access for every job category. Because school and work hours are the core obstacle for millions, changing the default election-day timetable still meaningfully reduces the barrier to voting and thus can improve turnout.

target: AG2's claim that holiday status is too narrow or negligible to matter much on turnout.
objection: A national holiday is not a trivial symbolic gesture. It changes the default timetable for schools and many workplaces, which directly lowers the scheduling friction that keeps people from voting. The objection assumes only paid leave matters, but the holiday also reorganizes the day around voting.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday is not an effective turnout lever and could leave low-income workers worse off.
objection: A holiday directly reduces the core barrier of rigid schedules and school/work conflicts, so it is not a negligible change. It alters the day people must vote on by putting schools and many workplaces into holiday mode, which makes participation easier rather than predictably worsening outcomes for low-income voters.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday is unreliable unless it guarantees paid leave.
objection: The mechanism is not limited to mandatory paid time off. Holiday status changes school routines and workplace expectations, which lowers the practical cost of voting and reduces scheduling obstacles for students, parents, and hourly workers even when some employers remain open.

target: AG2's claim that making Election Day a holiday would not reliably reduce barriers and might even harm low-income workers.
objection: The holiday is a meaningful access reform because it changes the school/workday structure that creates the conflict in the first place. By shifting the day into holiday mode and altering workplace norms, it reduces the scheduling burden for families and workers rather than inherently worsening their situation.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would be an unalloyed access improvement for low-income workers.
objection: A holiday could increase the practical time burden by concentrating more voters on the same day and producing longer polling-place lines and congestion. Low-income hourly workers are especially sensitive to total time away, so a holiday may offset some of its own scheduling benefit by increasing wait times.

target: AG2's claim that longer lines would necessarily outweigh the scheduling relief from a holiday.
objection: Wait time is only one component of the burden. The main problem is whether people can even be away during polling hours given work, school, and childcare obligations, and a holiday addresses that core scheduling conflict. In addition, election officials can plan staffing for the known holiday election day, so congestion is not an inevitable tradeoff.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status reliably reduces low-income workers' practical time burden.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably change the worker-level constraint that matters most: whether an employee can be away from a shift without losing wages. Private employers are still not required to provide paid, protected time to vote, so the holiday label may not materially reduce the real cost of voting for hourly workers; it can also leave polling congestion problems unresolved or harder to manage.
